Where it began

Ravi Shastri was born in Bombay on 27 May 1962 and went to Don Bosco High School in Matunga. The school was not known for its cricket, but in 1977, with Shastri as captain, it won the Giles Shield for the first time.

He was picked for Bombay in the Ranji Trophy in his last year at junior college, aged 17 years and 292 days, which made him at that point the youngest man to play for them. A couple of seasons later he was on a plane to New Zealand as a stand-in left-arm spinner. He reached Wellington on the eve of his first Test, and in New Zealand's second innings he took three wickets in four balls.

The player

Shastri played 80 Tests from 1981 to 1992, scoring 3,830 runs at 35.79 with 11 hundreds and taking 151 wickets. In the course of his career he batted everywhere from one to ten. He was part of the squad that won the 1983 World Cup, and in 1985 he was named Champion of Champions at the World Championship of Cricket in Australia, driving off with a new car as his prize.

His finest days with the bat came against the best. He made a hundred against the West Indian fast bowlers at Bridgetown in 1989, which he later thought his best innings, then 100 at Lord's and 187 at The Oval in 1990. On the 1991–92 tour of Australia he made 206 at Sydney, the first Test double hundred by an Indian against Australia. He captained India in a single Test, at Madras against the West Indies, and won it.

What made him special

Shastri stood six feet three and batted with great patience. His favourite stroke was a flick off the pads that people called the chapati, and against spin he was happy to hit over the top. Few men guarded their wicket more stubbornly.

At times the patience ran a little long, and crowds waiting for a boundary needed patience of their own. Yet when he chose to cut loose, few could match him. In January 1985, playing for Bombay against Baroda, he hit six sixes in an over, equalling Garry Sobers, and went on to what was then the fastest double hundred in first-class cricket.

Away from the middle

In England he spent four summers with Glamorgan, and in his last season at home he captained Bombay to the Ranji Trophy. An injury cut short his playing days at 31. He made his debut as a television commentator in 1995 and went on to call India's matches for many years. Later he was director of the Indian team and, from 2017 to 2021, its head coach.

He was given the Arjuna Award, and in 2024 he received the C. K. Nayudu Lifetime Achievement Award.

And finally

As a Test captain Shastri won every match he was in charge of. There was only one, but it is a record most captains would be glad to have.
